text: Stanford University hosts numerous centers and institutes focused on specific academic areas, which may be located within a department, across departments within a school, as an independent laboratory, or directly under the vice-provost and dean of research while remaining outside any school. Faculty involved in these centers must belong to a department within one of the university’s schools. These include Bio-X and Spectrum in Biological and Life Sciences; the Precourt Institute for Energy and Woods Institute for the Environment in Environmental Sciences; the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences (CASBS), the Center for the Study of Language and Information (CSLI), the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies (FSI), Human-Sciences and Technologies Advance Research Institute (H-STAR), Stanford Center on Longevity (SCL), Stanford Humanities Center, and the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research (SIEPR) in Humanities and Social Sciences; and in Physical Sciences, the Edward L. Ginzton Laboratory, the Geballe Laboratory for Advanced Materials, the Kavli Institute for Particle Astrophysics and Cosmology, Photon Ultrafast Laser Science and Engineering (PULSE), Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences (SIMES), and W. W. Hansen Experimental Physics Laboratory (HEPL). The Center for the Study of Language and Information (CSLI) is an independent research center founded in 1983 by philosophers, computer scientists, linguists, and psychologists from Stanford, SRI International, and Xerox PARC, aiming to study all forms of information and improve how humans and computers acquire and process it. It was initially funded by a $15 million grant from the System Development Foundation (SDF) for the Situated Language Project, reflecting the influence of situation semantics by John Perry and Jon Barwise, and this funding supported operations and the construction of Cordura Hall. Subsequent funding came from research grants and an industrial affiliates program. CSLI’s publications branch, founded and led by Dikran Karagueuzian, has become a key publisher in linguistics and related fields. Researchers associated with CSLI include Ronald Kaplan, Patrick Suppes, Edward N. Zalta, Keith Devlin, Solomon Feferman, Ivan Sag, Joan Bresnan, Annie Zaenen, Lauri Karttunen, Herb Clark, B. J. Fogg, and Clifford Nass. CSLI houses the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and previously hosted the Reuters Digital Vision Program. The Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies is a university-wide research and teaching institution dedicated to understanding international problems, policies, and institutions. It conducts interdisciplinary research, engages with policymakers globally, and trains scholars and future leaders. Teaching programs include the graduate-level Master of International Policy and honors programs in international security, democracy, development, and the rule of law. FSI is a full member of the Association of Professional Schools of International Affairs (APSIA). Its core and affiliated faculty come from diverse academic backgrounds including medicine, law, engineering, history, political science, economics, and sociology, with research focusing on governance, health policy, migration, development, and security, often examining regional dynamics in Asia, Europe, Africa, and Latin America. FSI was founded in 1987 following a faculty committee review that concluded Stanford should lead in international studies, encompassing interdisciplinary teaching, research, public service, and administration, under former president Richard Wall Lyman. It was initially named the Institute for International Studies and renamed the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies in 2005 after a $50 million gift from alumni Bradford M. Freeman and Ronald P. Spogli. Previous directors include Gerhard Casper, Coit D. Blacker, David Holloway, Walter Falcon, and Richard Lyman; the immediate past director was Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar, former Stanley Morrison Professor of Law at Stanford Law School and former official in the Obama and Clinton administrations, who served on the California Supreme Court and as president of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. FSI appoints faculty and research staff, funds research, directs projects, and sponsors lectures, policy seminars, and conferences. By tradition, it conducts joint faculty appointments across Stanford’s seven schools and draws faculty from various departments to pursue interdisciplinary research on international issues. The institute has 40 billeted faculty members—most with joint appointments—and 115 affiliated faculty with diverse academic perspectives. In addition to six major research centers, FSI sponsors the Ford Dorsey Master's in International Policy, the Inter-University Center for Japanese Language Studies, the Program on Energy & Sustainable Development, the Rural Education Action Program, the Stanford Center at Peking University, and the Stanford Program on International and Cross-Cultural Education. Founded in 1980, the Stanford Humanities Center is a multidisciplinary research institute advancing knowledge in culture, philosophy, history, and the arts. Since its founding, it has sponsored advanced research into the historical, philosophical, literary, artistic, and cultural dimensions of the human experience. Annual fellows, international visitors, research workshops, a digital humanities laboratory, and about fifty public events strengthen the university’s intellectual and creative life, foster interdisciplinary scholarship and teaching, and deepen understanding of shared humanity. The center offers approximately forty yearlong residential fellowships to scholars at various career stages. Each year, Stanford faculty and graduate students create fifteen diverse research workshops that challenge disciplinary boundaries, professionalizing graduate students by introducing them to academic conventions. Manuscript workshops assemble faculty experts to provide critical feedback to junior faculty preparing monographs. The center brings eminent scholars, public intellectuals, and critics to Stanford for lectures and interdisciplinary conferences, with past speakers including Isabel Allende, Roger Chartier, Stephen Jay Gould, Douglas Hofstadter, Gayatri Spivak, Marilynne Robinson, David Adjaye, David Eggers, and others. The Humanities Center, with the Center for Spatial and Textual Analysis (CESTA), expands humanities research and teaching through digital tools for discovery and dissemination. Short-term visitorships draw distinguished international scholars to share research. The center awards Hume Honors Fellowships to Stanford seniors writing honors theses in humanities departments; Hume Fellows reside for a year, contribute to the center’s community, and receive intellectual guidance. The Distinguished Careers Institute (DCI), established in 2014, is a year-long residential fellowship for about 20 individuals with established leadership careers, selected based on how their participation will shape future life journeys and their contributions to the program and global community. A collaboration among Stanford’s Office for Digital Education, the Department of Computer Science, and the Graduate School of Education established Stanford’s first dual-enrollment program for high school students from underrepresented backgrounds, which led to the creation of the Qualia Global Scholars Program. The Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (SAIL), also known as the Stanford AI Lab, is Stanford’s AI research laboratory. The current director is Professor Christopher D. Manning. SAIL was founded in 1963 by John McCarthy after he moved from MIT to Stanford; Lester D. "Les" Earnest, also from MIT, served as executive officer (self-deprecatingly, "Chief Bureaucrat") from 1965 to 1980. From 1966 to 1979, SAIL was housed in the D.C. Power building, named after Donald Clinton Power, who was president, CEO, and chairman of General Telephone & Electronics Corporation (later GTE) from 1951 to 1971. GT&E donated the unfinished building to Stanford after abandoning plans to establish a research center there. The building was located about 5 miles (8 km) from the main campus, at 1600 Arastradero Road, midway between Page Mill Road and Alpine Road, on a hill overlooking Felt Lake in the Santa Cruz Mountains, and was remote and rural, with an extreme 1960s architectural style, leading to a sense of isolation. Some staff reported feeling as if they were in the future. The building was demolished in 1986; as of 2003, the site is home to Portola Pastures, an equestrian center adjacent to the Arastradero Open Space Preserve. SAIL developed the WAITS operating system on a computer called SAIL, which ran on Digital Equipment Corporation PDP computers (PDP-6, KA10, KL10) and Foonly systems at CCRMA and LLL; the system was shut down in 1991. SAIL also developed the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Language (SAIL) in 1970 by Dan Swinehart and Bob Sproull. Around 1972, SAIL developed a computer-controlled vending machine, adapted from a machine rented from Canteen Vending, which sold beer, yogurt, and milk for cash or credit via a Teletype Model 33 KSR terminal. The machine, named the Prancing Pony after a room named after an inn in Tolkien’s Lord of the Rings, is still operational in the Computer Science Department with updated hardware and software. Alumni of the original SAIL played major roles in Silicon Valley firms, founding companies such as Cisco Systems, Sun Microsystems, Vicarm Inc. (acquired by Unimation), Foonly, Elxsi, Imagen, Xidex, Valid Logic Systems, and D.E. Shaw & Co. Research accomplishments include speech recognition and robotics. Notable former staff include Raj Reddy, Hans Moravec, Alan Kay, Victor Scheinman, Larry Tesler, Don Knuth, and Edward Feigenbaum. In 1979, SAIL’s activities were merged into the Computer Science Department and it moved to Margaret Jacks Hall on the main campus. After operating under the name Robotics Lab for over 15 years, SAIL was reinaugurated in 2004 in the Gates Computer Science Building with Sebastian Thrun as director. SAIL’s 21st-century mission is to “change the way we understand the world,” with research contributions in bioinformatics, cognition, computational geometry, computer vision, decision theory, distributed systems, game theory, general game playing, image processing, information retrieval, knowledge systems, logic, machine learning, multi-agent systems, natural language, neural networks, planning, probabilistic inference, sensor networks, and robotics. The best-known achievement of the new SAIL is the Stanley self-driving car that won the 2005 DARPA Grand Challenge. The Knowledge Systems Laboratory (KSL) was an AI research laboratory within the Department of Computer Science until 2007, located in the Gates Computer Science Building. The Center for Entrepreneurial Studies (CES) is a multidisciplinary business program for undergraduate and graduate students, incorporating courses from the School of Engineering and the Graduate School of Business, and the Stanford Mayfield Scholars Program, which offers select undergraduates business coursework and internships in high-tech startups. CES was founded by Tom Byers and Charles A. Holloway. The Stanford Center for Computer Research in Music and Acoustics (CCRMA), founded by John Chowning, is a multidisciplinary facility where composers and researchers collaborate using computer-based technology as both an artistic medium and research tool. CCRMA’s director is Chris Chafe; current faculty include musicians and engineers such as Julius Smith, Jonathan Berger, Max Mathews (emeritus), Ge Wang, Takako Fujioka, Tom Rossing, Jonathan Abel, Marina Bosi, David Berners, Patricia Alessandrini, Jay Kadis, and Fernando Lopez-Lezcano. Max Mathews died in 2011. CCRMA developed widely used digital sound synthesis techniques like FM synthesis and digital waveguide synthesis, with the FM synthesis patent bringing Stanford $20 million before expiration, making it the second most lucrative licensing agreement in Stanford’s history in 1994. CCRMA studies areas including composition, computer music, physical modeling, audio signal processing, sound recording and reproduction, psychoacoustics, acoustics, music information retrieval, audio networking, and spatial sound. It offers academic courses, seminars, small interest group meetings, summer workshops, and colloquia for the broader community and presents concerts of computer and experimental music regularly. The Knoll, a Spanish Gothic residence originally designed by Louis Christian Mullgardt for the university president, became home to the Music Department in 1946 and CCRMA in 1986. Damaged in the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake, CCRMA operated in the damaged building until a complete internal reconstruction between 2004 and 2005. The facility was reopened in spring 2005 with the CCRMA: newStage Festival, now housing several state-of-the-art music studios and top-tier research facilities for students, artists, and scientists. CCRMA is affiliated with the Center for Computer Assisted Research in the Humanities (CCARH), which conducts research on constructing computer databases for music and creating programs to access, analyze, print, and electronically perform music. The Stanford Institute for Creativity and the Arts (SiCa), established in 2006, serves as the core programmatic hub for the Stanford Arts Initiative, leading the development of new undergraduate arts programs, hosting artists in residence, awarding grants for multidisciplinary arts research and teaching, incubating collaborative performances and exhibitions with campus partners and other institutions, and providing centralized communication for arts events and programs. The Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering maintains the National Performance of Dams Program, a national database of structural and operational data on U.S. dam systems, begun in 1994. It provides data on both successful operations and incidents, including failures, to improve dam design, engineering processes, standards, operational procedures, guidelines, and public policy. The Michelle R. Clayman Institute for Gender Research, founded in 1974 and named after economist Michelle R. Clayman, is one of the nation’s oldest research organizations focused on gender. It designs interdisciplinary research, creates knowledge, networks people and ideas at Stanford, nationally, and internationally to promote gender equality. The institute brings together scholars and thought leaders from across disciplines to create knowledge and effect change. The building housing the Clayman Institute was renamed the Carolyn Lewis Attneave House in 2019; it was previously named Serra House after Junípero Serra. The institute was formed in 1972 by faculty and graduate students in the feminist movement, and in 1974, the Center for Research on Women (CROW) was established as the first interdisciplinary center of its kind under Myra Strober, the founding director. The reputation of the institute grew beyond Stanford, and the University of Chicago is mentioned in the context of its influence.

Founded in 1974 and named after economist Michelle R. Clayman, the Michelle R. Clayman Institute for Gender Research at Stanford University is one of the nation's oldest research organizations focused on the study of gender. The institute designs basic interdisciplinary research, creates knowledge, networks people and ideas at Stanford, nationally, and internationally to effect change and promote gender equality. It plays an integral role in the Stanford community by bringing together local, national, and international scholars and thought leaders from across disciplines to create knowledge and effect change. The institute's location was renamed the Carolyn Lewis Attneave House in 2019, formerly known as Serra House after Junípero Serra. In 1972, faculty and graduate students in the feminist movement were the impetus behind its formation. In 1974, the Center for Research on Women (CROW) was established as the first interdisciplinary center of its kind and quickly built a strong reputation under the direction of Myra Strober, the founding Director. The institute's reputation extended beyond Stanford, with the University of Chicago Press selecting Stanford as the base for the second five-year rotation of its interdisciplinary journal, Signs. In 1983, the institute was renamed the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and expanded its gender conversation through the "Difficult Dialogues" program, which ran from the 1990s through 2004. In 2004, Professor Londa Schiebinger, a historian of science, formed a plan to create research initiatives on gender issues, supported by a fellowship program, to attract scholars from Stanford and abroad. With matching funds from the Hewlett Foundation and strong support from the institute's Advisory Council, Schiebinger led a fundraising drive to create an endowment. IRWG was renamed in honor of Michelle R. Clayman, the major donor in the campaign, who serves as chair of the institute's Advisory Council. The Clayman Institute designs basic research and supports knowledge creation through its Fellowships and interdisciplinary programs. Recent reports and publications include: the institute runs two fellowship programs—the Faculty Research Fellowships, which seek to drive intellectual and social innovation through interdisciplinary gender studies, including residential fellowships for tenured, tenure-track, and postdoctoral scholars from Stanford and U.S. and foreign universities, and the Graduate Dissertation Fellowships for Stanford doctoral students in the writing stages of their dissertations whose research focuses on women and/or gender. Stanford is home to the Martin Luther King Jr. Research and Education Institute, which grew out of and still contains the Martin Luther King Jr. Papers Project, a collaboration with the King Center to publish the King papers held by the King Center. The Stanford Internet Observatory, established in 2019 as a multidisciplinary program for the study of abuse in information technologies with a focus on social media, is part of the Stanford Cyber Policy Center, a joint initiative of the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies and Stanford Law School. The Observatory has identified the Russian government's online involvement in global elections since its inception. Projects such as the "Virality Project" have been criticized as censorship since the release of the Twitter files by some students, Matt Taibbi, and others outside the university. Stanford HAI was founded in 2019 by Fei-Fei Li, John Etchemendy, James Landay, and Chris Manning. HAI's mission is to advance AI research that prioritizes human well-being, fostering collaboration across disciplines to ensure AI is developed ethically and inclusively. In its first five years, HAI directed over $40 million into AI research, supported over 300 scholars, and launched specialized centers such as the Stanford Digital Economy Lab and the Center for Research on Foundation Models. The institute has also fostered partnerships with policymakers and industry leaders, advocating for the democratization of AI research. HAI continues to push for new models of collaboration, emphasizing the need for large-scale resources to address the growing complexity of AI systems. The Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI) plays a crucial role in Governor Gavin Newsom's efforts to ensure the safe and responsible development of artificial intelligence (AI) in California. Dr. Fei-Fei Li, co-director of Stanford HAI, has been a key figure in advising the state on AI policy, contributing to initiatives aimed at balancing innovation with risk mitigation. Building on the partnership established by Newsom's 2023 executive order, the Governor has called upon Stanford HAI to continue its leadership in developing empirical, science-based guidelines for the deployment of generative AI (GenAI). This future work will focus on assessing the potential risks and benefits of frontier AI models, crafting adaptive policies, and ensuring that California remains at the forefront of AI governance. Newsom's administration relies on HAI's expertise to navigate AI's rapid advancements while protecting the public from potential harms. Stanford's Center for Computer Research and Acoustics is part of a consortium with CNMAT and the Institut de Recherche et Coordination Acoustique/Musique (IRCAM) in Paris.
